newsitem.title: USA: DOLLAR ENDS WEAKER IN US ON ISSING, WALL ST SLIDE.
newsitem.headline: DOLLAR ENDS WEAKER IN US ON ISSING, WALL ST SLIDE.

text.p: The dollar slumped broadly throughout U.S. trade, ending lower as European players took profits before the weekend and a German central banker warned of inflation pressures, analysts said.
A heavy selloff in U.S. stocks and bonds compounded the dollar's woes, contributing to the dollar's biggest one-day declines in three months, analysts said.
"This was a correction, and a big one. Everybody was long in the dollar and U.S. assets," said Andrew Hodge, financial strategist at Bank Brussels Lambert in New York.

Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing was quoted by Germany's Boersen-Zeitung newspaper as saying German price developments were moving in the wrong direction, suggesting the central bank might raise interest rates to bolster the mark.
Issing, who on Tuesday said the Bundesbank was worried about dollar/mark's rapid rise, also said domestic monetary policy goals outweigh pan-European issues at the Bundesbank.
"The Germans were sounding fairly aggressive about the dollar and inflation. We were already spiralling down and that added another kick," said Hodge.
Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke overnight reiterated that the central bank would prefer a dollar/mark rate near 1.70.
The dollar fell to 1.8450/60 marks from 1.8600/05 at the open, and its 24-hour drop of over two pfennigs was the biggest since May 20.
Against the yen, the dollar fell to 114.75/85 from 117.22/27 and the 3.7-yen decline since Thursday's close was the largest since May 7.
The British pound fell sharply for a second straight day, indirectly boosting the yen and mark against the dollar.

The pound has fallen nearly five percent against the mark this week, particularly hurt when the Bank of England indicated its fourth consecutive monthly increase in official interest rates could be the last for some time.
Higher interest rates tend to boost a currency making investments denominated in that currency more attractive.

"Sterling was under severe pressure in early trade and a lot of what's happened to the dollar is related to what's happened in sterling," said Michael Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.

The big drop on Wall Street, where the Dow Jones industrials shed 156 points, or 1.9 percent, and the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond fell 1-16/32 points, exacerbated the dollar's slide, analysts said.
"Stocks were down 200 points for a while, which made things hard on the dollar," said Malpede.
European operators booking profits as their week ended near U.S. midday caused the dollar to sink sharply, dealers said.
"It looks like a lot of people that were long dollars from very good levels decided to take some profits," said Brian McClave, senior trader at Sanwa Bank Ltd New York.

The dollar weakened in Asia after Japan reported its current account surplus--the broadest measure of trade in goods and services--rose 56 percent in June from a year earlier, to over one trillion yen.
"The dollar's fall against the yen was related to the current account figures. There are a lot of current concerns about trade," Malpede said.
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.5092/02 Swiss francs from 1.5208/18 at the open and to Canadian $1.3901/06 from C$1.3905/10.
Sterling rose to $1.5870/80 from $1.5758/68. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7343/48 from $0.7296/01 at the open.
((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
